items.title: Al Rose Interview, 1975-02-19
items.q: I got hold of Sidney Bechet... I called Bechet and he suggested Sidney D. Paris and Gate Mouth. And so, I just made a deal with him to bring him in... we had the jazz concert where tickets were sold... we did have Jack D. Garden and Bose and Fazola.

ctx.x: Because I lived here. But in getting out of town, when I went to college, I went to Temple University in Philadelphia. And at that time, I came with an enormous collection of phonograph records. Because I couldn't really see myself surviving through the period of a college education without the music. So I had this large collection of records. Now, it happened that this was a time of a reawakening of an interest in American popular music, especially among people who were interested in swing. But even among these…
Now, had you done any of this kind of thing before?

items.title: Al Rose Interview, 1976-02-19
items.q: I got hold of Sidney Bechet... I called Bechet and I, and he suggested Sidney D. Paris... I just made a deal with him to bring him in... That was Muggsy Spanier, Sidney Bechet... The same group that I brought on my Ivy League tour

ctx.x: But even among these people, there was a consciousness of the personalities and the people that had recorded the early jazz. Some of those people, of course, were playing in swing bands. And the fact that I had this collection became very well known in school, and people used to come to my room all the time to listen to records. And to discuss with me the music that they were playing, and they were much interested in this. Well, in 1935, the American Newspaper Guild was about to, was planning an annual affair.…
Now, had you done any of this kind of thing before?

items.title: Al Rose Interview, 1989-08-13
items.q: I was hiring people like Sidney Bechet and Muggsy Spanier, you know, for my regular concerts.

ctx.x: And it was a black theater and I used to come out of, out of class and go across the street to the theater all the time, because I knew a lot of the musicians that were, that were playing in the, in the show. And it was during the time when I had first started doing jazz concerts. So it was 1936 and I went backstage, because his band was playing there. And I knew Louis Russell and Red Allen and people that were playing there, Al Nicholas. So, I had, I had met Louis before, I don't actually remember when, but…
Okay, we're on the second reel. Al Rose, same date. August 13th, 1989. Okay, we left off with Eus... Eus Panassia.

items.title: Al Rose Interview, 1975-02-03
items.q: I was only, I always gave Bechet two or three solos to do in a concert on soprano sax.

ctx.x: I'm beginning to get the picture on you. So you, your activities date back before being in the jazz business, date back before Journeys into Jazz? Oh yes.

My first actual public activity in jazz was when I ran a jazz concert for the American Newspaper Guild in Philadelphia at Mercantile Hall. And that was in 1936, in January of 1936. And it included Sidney Bechet and Sidney D. Paris, members of Jack Teagarden's band who were playing upstairs for dancing. That included Sterling Boze and Boze and Irving Fazola. And a local clarinet player by the name of Billy Kretschmer was there. As far as I know, this is the first actual concert ever held of authentic jazz in which…
Oh. What about, did you, did you have any trouble, uh, getting in? Have I, didn't you tell me something about that once? Are you, people didn't recognize you as the producer?
